papers.title_in_file: Combinatorial optimization with quantum imaginary time evolution
papers.version_note: arXiv:2312.16664v1, dated December 29, 2023. The text layer lost the summation limits and layout of Eqs. (7) to (17); the prose around each equation was read. The paper's own text and the Fig. 5 caption differ on the number of initial states and the largest LABS size (see labs-test-setup).
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of quantum imaginary time evolution with a separable linear Ansatz (and a small test of a quadratic entangling Ansatz) on weighted MaxCut against the Goemans-Williamson algorithm and on LABS against QAOA values from another study.

existing.note: The paper states this three times (Introduction, Section III and the Conclusion) about the separable (linear) Ansatz. It states it without a proof or a cost bound.
quotes: Our separable Ansatz can be simulated efficiently classically.
QITE with a linear Ansatz can be simulated efficiently classically, so the computation can be done for larger graph sizes than considered here without issue.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit on their own method in the Conclusion (Section V, p.7) and in Section III (p.5).
existing.reader_inference: The paper gives no proof or complexity bound for the statement. It rests on the product-state start and the commuting single-qubit updates of Section II.

existing.note: The paper limits the comparison. It compares the AVERAGE probability of measuring the ground state, P(GS), of linear Ansatz QITE with 40 steps to p = 10 QAOA values taken from Ref. [23] (not re-run), for problem sizes 6 to 18 (Fig. 6). The best case P(GS) is higher than the QAOA values. The entangling quadratic Ansatz was tested only up to N = 9, where it gave a P(GS) no more than 10% higher, so the no-advantage statement covers that range only.
existing.value: The authors report that the average probability of measuring the ground state, P(GS), of linear Ansatz QITE with 40 steps was comparable to p = 10 QAOA, taking the QAOA values from Ref. [23], for problem size 6 ≤ N ≤ 18, and that the best case P(GS) was consistently higher than the QAOA results. They report that the entangling Ansatz gave a P(GS) no more than 10% higher than the linear Ansatz for problem sizes up to N = 9, and that they do not see a significant advantage with an entangling Ansatz.

existing.note: The paper limits it. 'Often outperforms' holds for the BEST approximation ratio over trials (above 1 for 25 and 50 steps and N > 10), after a sufficient number of steps; the average ratio is below 1 (about 0.90 to 0.96; about 0.95 for N > 100). The result is for weighted Newman-Watts-Strogatz graphs with k = 4 and p = 0.5, one imaginary-time-dependent (ITD) edge, and the comparison is against the lowest energy GW produced. 10 steps were not enough.
existing.value: The authors report that QITE with a linear (separable) Ansatz and 1 ITD edge on weighted Newman-Watts-Strogatz graphs with k = 4 and p = 0.5, up to 150 vertices, often outperforms the GW algorithm after a sufficient number of steps. They report that the best approximation ratio for 25 and 50 steps remains above 1 for N > 10, while the average approximation ratio is about 0.95 for N > 100 vertices.

existing.reader_inference: The approximation ratio (AR) is QITE energy divided by the lowest GW energy, and GW is not guaranteed to reach the ground state at large N (Section III). An AR below 1 on average means QITE is on average not better than GW. The 'outperforms' result is a best-of-trials result.
